phonemes.desc: Voiceless bilabial stop [p], as in English 'spur'.
Short open-mid front [ɛ], the reduced vowel of the first syllable.
Trilled or tapped r, close back [u], final voiced dental n; the name is the Common Slavic agent noun built on the root *per- 'to strike'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PER-un' with a rolled r; the name is an agent noun meaning 'Striker'.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *per-/*perkw- 'to strike, to thunder'; the same root family behind Lithuanian Perkūnas and Vedic Parjanya (Toporov; Mallory & Adams)

kin.label: Baltic
kin.form: Lithuanian Perkūnas, Latvian Pērkons — the Baltic thunderers, closest linguistic relatives of the name

kin.label: Proposed
kin.form: Latin quercus 'oak' and Gothic fairguni 'mountain' have been compared to the *perkw- root; the connection is traditional but debated

pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Perun preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive non-ASCII letter — so the temple stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule.

domains.title: Perun
domains.subtitle: Thunder
domains.lead: Perun is the thunderer of the Slavs: god of lightning, storm, and the sacred oak, patron of warriors and guarantor of oaths. His name means 'striker.' The East Slavic chronicles place him first among the gods of Kyiv, and folklore kept his axe, his fire, and his wrath alive long after the idols sank in the Dnieper.

cards.name: The Striker
cards.desc: His weapons are the thunderbolt and the throwing axe; lightning is his signature in every early description of the cult.

cards.name: The Sacred Oak
cards.desc: Oaks struck by lightning were his; a perpetual fire burned for him on open hilltop sanctuaries such as Peryn' near Novgorod.

cards.name: Lord of Oaths
cards.desc: The Rus'-Byzantine treaties swore by Perun and Volos; the perjurer's written curse was death by his own weapons.

cards.name: Enemy of Veles
cards.desc: In the reconstructed myth-cycle he pursues the cattle-thief Veles down through the tiers of the world-tree.

symbols.name: Throwing axe / thunderbolt
symbols.meaning: His striking weapon, worn in miniature on amulets and incised on stones across the Slavic world

symbols.name: Oak and perpetual fire
symbols.meaning: The lightning-struck tree and the hilltop flame kept burning in his honor at open-air shrines

symbols.name: Thunderstone (gromovik)
symbols.meaning: Fossil belemnites kept in Slavic households against lightning, understood as his spent arrows

symbols.name: The sacred hill
symbols.meaning: Kyiv's shrine hill and Novgorod's Peryn' — high ground set apart for his unroofed cult

symbols.name: Elijah's fiery chariot
symbols.meaning: The Christian successor-image that inherited his storm: wheels of fire crossing the sky

mythology.lead: The stories of Perun survive mostly at second hand, through the chronicles of his enemies and the reconstructions of modern philologists. From them emerges a thunderer who is at once war-god and covenant-god: he hurls the bolt, he guards the sworn word, and he wages an eternal feud with Veles, lord of the underworld and the herd.

myths.title: The Idols on the Hill
myths.text: The Povest' vremennykh let ('Tale of Bygone Years') reports that Prince Vladimir, before his conversion, set up idols on a hill outside Kyiv: Perun of wood with a head of silver and a moustache of gold, flanked by Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh, and the people were commanded to sacrifice to them. In 988 the idols were beaten with sticks and thrown into the Dnieper, and the chronicler records that the people waded into the river weeping, 'for they had not yet been baptized, but were baptized in the name of Perun.' The detail is priceless: the Church's own founding history admits that Rus' wept for the thunderer as it left him. Conversion was not a serene enlightenment but a national funeral — and Perun was the body. The idol sank; the oath, as the treaty of 944 shows, floated for another half-century.

myths.title: Sworn by Their Own Weapons
myths.text: The text of Prince Igor's treaty with Byzantium, preserved in the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6452/944), embeds the old oath formula verbatim. For the clauses of war and peace the Rus' swear by Perun — and by Volos, the cattle god, for everything touching livestock — and the curse on the perjurer is physical and total: may he be destroyed by his own weapons, unprotected by his own shield, slain by his own sword, shot by his own arrows. The same formula recurs in the treaty of 971, scaled down but recognizable. Here Perun functions exactly as Zeus Horkios does in Hesiod: not a god of stories but the installed enforcer of agreements between peoples. A thunderer who witnesses contracts is a thunderer whose violence has been socialized — order made audible.

myths.title: The Sorcerers' Revolt
myths.text: Nearly a century after the baptism of Rus', the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6579/1071) records a four-day uprising in Novgorod. Wandering volkhvy — sorcerers — declared that Perun had spoken: the powerful were hoarding grain while the common people starved, and the god demanded that the guilty be put to death. A crowd dragged officials through the streets, killed some, and threatened worse until the city governor's men cut down the ringleaders. The episode is one of the last organized flickers of resistance to Christianization, and it shows what Perun meant to those who invoked him: not a temple idol but a voice of communal justice, claimed by street prophets against the new Christian order. A god can be outlawed from every altar and still be quoted by the poor — that is what 'lord of oaths' means when the oath is broken from above.

myths.title: The One God of the Slavs
myths.text: The earliest written notice of the Slavic thunderer comes from Procopius of Caesarea, Wars 7.14 (c. 550): the Slavs 'consider that one god, the maker of lightning, is alone lord of all things, and they sacrifice to him cattle and all other victims; and they reverence also rivers and nymphs and all sorts of other beings.' Procopius does not give the god's name — but the identification with Perun, whose very name means 'striker', is the standard and near-certain reading, and the passage is regularly cited as the thunderer's baptism into history, six centuries before Kyiv's idols. It also sketches the whole divine household at once: a supreme bolt-hurler above, and beneath him the wet, local, numerous powers that Veles would later rule. The sixth-century sky already holds the shape of the tenth-century pantheon.

myths.title: The Eternal Pursuit of Veles
myths.text: The central cycle of Slavic mythology survives in no manuscript; it was reconstructed by Vyacheslav Ivanov and Vladimir Toporov from the pairing of the gods in chronicle oaths, wedding laments, seasonal rites, and the comparative pattern of the Indo-European storm-combat. In their model, Veles — lord of the underworld, cattle, and wealth — commits a theft against the sky: Perun's cattle, his treasure, sometimes his bride. Perun pursues him down the tiers of the world-tree, hurling bolts; Veles transforms and wriggles — serpent, catfish, black eel — and each spring the thunderer strikes him down, and the rain returns to the herds. The scholars were explicit that they were reconstructing, and the honesty should be kept: this is a hypothesis, not an epic. But the pieces fit with unusual stubbornness, and no rival account explains the oath-pairing so economically.

lore.syncretism: Christianization did not erase Perun; it reassigned him. His functions passed chiefly to the prophet Elijah — Il'ya — whose fiery chariot crosses the sky in Russian folklore, whose day kept the thunderer's weather, and whose icons still stand in village fields against storm and fire. Saint George absorbed something of the dragon-slaying warrior. Byzantine-educated writers performed the usual interpretatio, reading Perun as a Slavic Zeus, while comparative scholarship has added Thor and Indra as cousins through the shared inheritance of the storm-combat myth. In the twentieth century Perun returned openly: Slavic Native Faith movements restored his name, his day, and his hilltop fires, and he now stands — as the chronicles always placed him — first among the gods. Of all the drowned pantheon, he alone kept a national audience.
lore.culturalLegacy: Perun never left the languages. The word itself became the poetic Slavic name for thunder — Polish piorun is the everyday word for a thunderbolt, and Russian keeps perun in elevated speech — while Lithuanian Perkūnas keeps the cognate alive next door. Folklore preserved his attributes as 'thunderstones,' fossil belemnites (gromovik) hung in houses against lightning, and the epic hero Il'ya Muromets rides in his shadow with a mace that is really a bolt. In the modern period Perun has become an emblem of Slavic identity: he heads the pantheon of Rodnover and Native Faith communities from Ukraine to Poland, lends his name to military units, rockets, and football terraces, and appears wherever the question is asked what a pre-Christian Slavic civilization would have honored. The Church feared him for a reason: of all the Kyiv gods, his name proved the hardest to drown.
lore.extendedMeditation: Perun is the god of the strike — the moment when the sky asserts itself against the earth and the forest smells of split wood. Everything about him is vertical: the bolt falls, the oak points up, the oath rises to the witness who will enforce it. He is violent, but his violence is legal: he does not rage, he executes. That is why treaties trusted him and why rebels in 1071 invoked him against hoarding governors; he is the enforcer of an order older than any prince. To study Perun is to watch a society argue with its own thunder. The chroniclers beat his idol with sticks and threw it in the river, then preserved his name more carefully than any priest had — in oath-texts, in curses, in the weeping of the baptized. A god whose worshippers cry when he leaves has not been defeated; he has been internalized. Perun endures as the sound above the roof that still makes everyone, believer or not, look up.
lore.archaeology: The clearest material footprint of Perun's cult is Peryn', a rounded hill at the bend of the Volkhov south of Novgorod, excavated by G. Lebedev's team in the 1950s: a circular ritual enclosure with a stone- and clay-lined platform, dated to the tenth–twelfth centuries, on a site whose very name derives from the god. No temple building was found — the open-air precinct fits the chronicle image of a hill shrine — but the enclosure's planned geometry and burnt deposits mark organized, funded cult practice. Across the Slavic world, miniature axe-amulets ('thunder-axes on chains') and axe-mark graffiti are read as Perun's weapon in miniature, though none is inscribed. The Kyiv hill of 988 has never been securely located archaeologically, and the enigmatic four-sided Zbruch idol is more often assigned to Svetovit than to the thunderer. Direct evidence is thin — but Peryn' proves the cult was real.
